key_insight: Vision-language models can predict artistic style using a mix of visual and textual cues, but their internal criteria only partially align with how art historians reason about style—revealing both meaningful overlaps and systematic differences.
problem_solved: Clarifies what cues VLMs use to recognize artistic style and assesses whether those cues correspond to art-historical criteria, addressing the interpretability gap between model predictions and humanities expertise.
method: Apply interpretability tools (attention/grad maps, concept probing) to VLMs to identify visual and textual features driving style predictions.
Compare model-derived cues against art-historical annotations and criteria via collaboration with art historians to evaluate alignment and divergence.
Quantify and visualize sources of agreement and bias (e.g., color, texture, composition, metadata) to explain when and why models succeed or fail.
impact: Helps practitioners build more transparent, reliable multimodal systems for cultural heritage and fine-grained visual tasks, and guides dataset curation and model evaluation by surfacing domain-specific failure modes.
visual_elements: Overlay examples: attention/heatmap overlays on paintings showing regions the VLM uses for style labels versus annotated art-historian focal points.
Bar chart: feature-importance comparison (color, texture, composition, subject matter, metadata) for model vs. art-historian ratings.
Confusion matrix: style classification errors highlighting systematic confusions and dataset biases across artistic movements.
Schematic: pipeline diagram showing VLM inputs, interpretability analyses, and the human-in-the-loop evaluation with art-history experts.
paper_title: Does AI See like Art Historians? Interpreting How Vision Language Models Recognize Artistic Style
paper_authors: Marvin Limpijankit, Milad Alshomary, Yassin Oulad Daoud, Amith Ananthram, Tim Trombley
